articles.title: How flydubai security failure, across 3 countries, almost led to 'Israel’s 9/11’
articles.summary: A string of security failures across Oman, the UAE and Israel allowed the flydubai co-pilot to get into the cockpit, a Wall Street Journal investigation
articles.body: A string of security failures across Oman, the UAE and Israel allowed the flydubai co-pilot to get into the cockpit, a Wall Street Journal investigation has found. The lapses nearly led to an aviation disaster reminiscent of 9/11, despite authorities having reasons to be concerned about him.The failures began in Oman, where authorities had scrutinised Hamam al-Hammami’s online activity and found he showed too much interest in radical ideology to be trusted as a pilot at state carrier Oman Air. They banned him from flying, sent him to a deradicalisation programme and moved him to a desk job, but did not broadly communicate their concerns about him.Oman flagged him, but the warning did not travelWhen al-Hammami joined flydubai in February, the airline did not contact Oman to vet his previous experience, the WSJ reported. It conducted a criminal-background check, but the earlier concerns that had led Oman to remove him from flying were not passed on to the new employer. The operator, flydubai, later assigned him to the sensitive Tel Aviv route, which he flew multiple times.Oman’s handling of the case also created another missed opportunity. People familiar with the matter said that had the country formally withdrawn al-Hammami’s pilot licence over its concerns, the action would likely have been flagged to the UAE. Instead, the concerns about his extremism were not communicated more widely.Israel had his name, and still let him flyThe final layer of failures came in Israel, where foreign airlines are required to submit passenger and crew lists before arriving.Airline operator flydubai had submitted the manifest for Flight 1073, but Israel’s transportation ministry said it did not believe it had the authority or expertise to vet foreign flight crews. The ministry also said it had never asked to access a database created in 2023 to help authorised agencies review passenger and crew information because it did not know the database was operational or that it could use it.There was an even more basic warning that should have stopped al-Hammami from flying to Israel. Pilots from countries such as Oman, which does not have diplomatic relations with Israel, are barred from flying to the country. Yet al-Hammami was allowed onto the Tel Aviv-bound flight.Israel’s own previous warnings also raise questions about how the system failed. A classified May 2024 report by the country’s comptroller general had warned that aviation security had grown lax, with fragmented responsibilities and unclear lines of authority. The report also identified manpower and budget problems affecting oversight by the transportation ministry.The cockpit attackThe security failures culminated halfway through Flight 1073, when al-Hammami attacked Captain Smit Machchhar with an emergency axe after excusing himself to pray.The wounded captain managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and others to enter and overpower the co-pilot. They then helped pull the aircraft out of a dangerous dive.The UAE’s attorney general has described the incident as an attempted terrorist act. Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Israel suspect al-Hammami was trying to crash the aircraft in Tel Aviv, according to people familiar with their thinking. All three countries are investigating whether he acted alone; so far, investigators have not found links to a foreign power or major terrorist organisation, those people said.The incident has since prompted Israel to review the security of foreign airline flights to the country.You use AI every day. articles.title: Guam's snake invasion became so bad that power lines were a problem: How brown tree snakes climbed poles, caused blackouts and forced researchers to find bizarre ways to keep them away
articles.summary: Guam’s brown tree snake problem is far stranger than a typical invasive-species story.
articles.body: Guam’s brown tree snake problem is far stranger than a typical invasive-species story. The snakes did not simply spread through forests and prey on native wildlife. They learned to exploit the island’s infrastructure too, climbing poles, reaching electrical equipment and triggering costly power failures.The brown treesnake (Boiga irregularis) arrived on Guam sometime after World War II, probably as a stowaway in cargo. With few natural controls and plenty of prey, its population exploded. The consequences were severe for native birds and eventually reached something far less wild: the electrical grid.When a snake became an electrical problemBrown tree snakes are excellent climbers. They can move onto guy wires, poles, transformers and other electrical structures. When a snake touches two electrical points at once, its body can effectively bridge the circuit.The result can be a short circuit, electrical fault or surge. The snake may be electrocuted, while transformers and other equipment can also be damaged.The problem is not new. More than 1,600 snake-caused outages were recorded between 1978 and 1997, and older estimates put the annual economic impact at more than $4.5 million over a seven-year period.The snake that found a way around barriersThe strangest part came when researchers tried to stop the snakes from climbing smooth cylinders.Scientists discovered that brown tree snakes could form their bodies into a loop resembling a lasso. They use that loop as an anchor, then make small waves with the rest of the body to inch upward.Researchers named this previously undocumented movement “lasso locomotion.” It allows the snakes to climb smooth, wide cylinders that would defeat more conventional climbing movements. The discovery also explained why some seemingly clever barriers were not as snake-proof as expected.Then came the parachuting miceGuam’s snake-control efforts have produced one of the strangest wildlife-control methods ever attempted.Researchers discovered that acetaminophen is toxic to brown tree snakes. Instead of scattering bait across the forest floor, wildlife managers developed a way to place treated dead mice high in the canopy, where the snakes naturally hunt.Helicopters were used to release dead mice containing acetaminophen. Small cardboard-and-paper devices slowed their descent and helped the baits become caught in vegetation rather than simply falling to the ground.The method was designed to target snakes while reducing exposure to other wildlife. It has been used as a targeted control tool, not as a solution capable of eliminating Guam’s entire snake population.Dogs, traps and better barriers joined the fightThere is no single fix for an invasion this deeply established. Researchers have therefore tried several approaches, including traps, improved barriers, toxic baits and detection methods.Specially trained detector dogs can help locate brown tree snakes, while rapid-response teams work to intercept snakes that may leave Guam aboard ships or aircraft. That matters because Guam is a major Pacific transportation hub, making accidental spread to places such as Hawaii and the Northern Mariana Islands a continuing concern.The brown tree snake story shows how an invasive animal can reshape an island far beyond its forests.It has been linked to the decline or local extinction of many native bird species. It has disrupted electrical infrastructure and created an expensive maintenance problem. And its ability to hitchhike in cargo means Guam's problem could become another island's problem if prevention fails.Perhaps the most striking lesson is that wildlife does not always stay on the side of the landscape humans consider “natural.” On Guam, the snake adapted to poles, wires and other structures with surprising ease. The response had to become equally inventive.Disclaimer: This article is based on information from the U.S. Geological Survey and published scientific research. Control methods described above are specialized wildlife-management techniques and should not be attempted by the public.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Radical change needed to cut Scottish child poverty, says charity
articles.summary: The Joseph Rowntree Foundation says Scotland is on course to miss legally-binding poverty targets "by a wide margin".
articles.body:
Scotland is on course to miss legally-binding targets to cut child poverty "by a wide margin", according to a report from a leading social reform charity.

The Joseph Rowntree Foundation (JRF) said one in five children was in poverty and "radical change" was needed to put the Scottish government's pledges back on track.

It urged ministers to craft a "much bolder and properly-funded plan to reduce poverty" by rewiring local government, public services and the tax system.

The Scottish government said it had made great strides, with its policies keeping 100,000 children out of poverty this year, but accepted there was more to do.

In 2017, MSPs passed a law requiring ministers to hit four targets , including pushing the share of children in relative poverty below 10% by 2030.

But the JRF's Poverty in Scotland report found the figure remained stubbornly high, averaging 21% from 2022 to 2025. The UK average is 28%.

Relative poverty means a household has disposable income after housing costs below 60% of the UK median, adjusted for family size and composition.

Overall, the report concluded, 940,000 people in Scotland were in relative poverty – 17% of the population.

The charity said that "despite some progress" the Scottish government's existing plans "will not deliver the scale of change needed to shift the dial."

Reasons for the failure were "complex", it said, but could include UK government austerity, a cost of living crisis, and "a dysfunctional relationship between local and national government in Scotland."

Scotland's Social Justice and Housing Secretary, Shirley-Anne Somerville, is currently overseeing a review of the poverty reduction goals after some interim targets were missed and data collection was adjusted, complicating the ability to assess progress.

The targets are based on annual figures which can be volatile but JRF and the Scottish government agree that three-year averages are more useful .

The JRF urged Somerville not to weaken the goals but to set "stretching, statutory, income-based poverty-reduction targets, with strong accountability measures".

From day one in the job, the issue has been at the heart of John Swinney's personal political project.

"My overriding priority will be to work to eradicate child poverty in Scotland," he told me in his first interview as first minister, minutes after being sworn in at the Court of Session in Edinburgh in 2024.

In his successful campaign to retain power at this year's Holyrood election , the Scottish National Party leader repeated his "determination to eradicate child poverty."

But the JRF says there is now an "increasing disconnect" between such rhetoric and "the reality of life for families in poverty across Scotland."

Its report said relative poverty rates were highest – at 47% – for children in ethnic minority families.

It added that 11% of Scotland's overall population was defined as being in deep poverty and 7% in very deep poverty.

In a statement issued in advance of the report's publication, Shirley-Anne Somerville said the Scottish child payment was "providing unparalleled financial support to the families of over 320,000 children."

The Scottish government would do more, she said, by expanding breakfast clubs for children and investing more than £40m in improving access to transport and skills for parents.

"Overall in 2026-27 we are committing around £3.5bn to policies that tackle poverty and the cost of living," she added.

Scotland misses targets on reducing child poverty

Swinney to make eradicating child poverty greatest priority

The JRF report suggests the following policies can help to reduce poverty.

Create flexible, well-paid jobs , especially in parts of Scotland where people cannot find work within easy reach of their homes

Expand access to high-quality, affordable childcare with the flexibility to allow parents in low-income families to work

Ensure adequate levels of payments, especially for people with disabilities who may have to fund their own care

Maintain and improve provision of social and affordable housing , which has helped Scotland keep its poverty rate below the UK average

The report focused on the "critical role" of Scotland's 32 councils in reducing poverty, noting that local government is in the early stages of a big shake up .

"Councils are not doing enough," it concludes, "with people on low incomes and living in more deprived areas reporting worse experiences of services and higher levels of disaffection."

The report urges Swinney's government to embrace the opportunity to craft "refitted" councils which can play a fuller role in poverty reduction, in partnership with the third sector.

This, it says, requires reform not just of local government's structure but of its funding, including the "regressive" council tax which "takes up a much larger proportion of low-income households' budgets than better-off households'."

Funding of councils, says the JRF, is "stretched to breaking point", with the current model "increasingly unfit for purpose" and "hampering local efforts to reduce poverty".

"Years of austerity, shifting goalposts from the Scottish government, single-year budgets and an ever-blooming number of strategies and action plans mean councils are often acting with one hand tied behind their back," says the report.

In her statement, Somerville said tackling poverty was at the heart of the Scottish government's plans for public service reform including tailoring services for individual needs in an approach known as "whole-family support".

"The time to go further is now," she said. "That means changing how services work together, ensuring they are joined up and designed around need, so that families can get the right support, at the right time and in the right place."

The JRF describes the current roll-out and funding for whole-family support as "wholly inadequate."

In a statement, Cosla, which represents local authorities, said its members took the report seriously and would do everything possible to cut poverty.

But its resources spokesperson, Kelly Parry, said councils were being constrained by funding shortages and rising demand for services.

Opinion polling conducted by the Diffley Partnership for the JRF suggests that two thirds of people think their council is underfunded, with just 4% saying the opposite.

It also indicates that people significantly underestimate the 61% share of local government funding which comes directly from the Scottish government. Council tax, by contrast, accounts for just 17%.

The pollster surveyed 3,381 adults in Scotland between 22 and 26 June.

"Councils are ready to be held accountable for the contribution we make," added Parry.

"But responsibility must be matched by the powers, fair and flexible multi-year funding, and genuine partnership needed to deliver lasting change."

articles.title: Nolo changes from a hurricane to a typhoon after crossing the international date line
articles.summary: Nolo has changed from a strong hurricane to a typhoon after it crossed the international date line.
articles.body: MIAMI — Nolo has changed from a strong hurricane to a typhoon after it crossed the international date line. Nolo was a Category 3 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 115 mph (185 kph) Sunday morning Hawaii time before it crossed the agreed-upon line in the Pacific Ocean that separates one day from the next. Names of tropical cyclones vary by the parts of the world where they occur. Monday morning Japan time, Typhoon Nolo had maximum sustained winds of 100 mph (162 kph) and was moving west at 19 mph (30 kph), according to the Japan Meteorological Agency. “The good news is there’s a large, vast ocean, so even though it is still going to be strong, it’s not near any land,” said John Cangialosi, a senior hurricane specialist with the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami. Tropical cyclones with winds over 74 mph (119 kph) are called hurricanes in the northern Atlantic Ocean and the central and eastern Pacific. They are typhoons in the North Pacific, while the South Pacific and Indian Ocean use just the generic term tropical cyclone no matter the strength of the storm. Nolo is forecast to keep moving west and gradually weaken. Nolo skirted Hawaii as a hurricane a week ago. It then lost some of its punch and became a tropical storm, before regaining hurricane strength on Friday. Elsewhere in the Pacific, Hurricane Rachel continued heading westward on a path away from Mexico. As the storm moved further out to sea, it was sending dangerous waves and swells back to the coast of west-central Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula, according to the hurricane center.

articles.title: Key takeaways as Brazil heads to presidential runoff that could reshape Latin America
articles.summary: Brazil is heading for another Lula-Bolsonaro showdown. But this time it is Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son Flávio who stands between leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and another term in power. A Bolsonaro victory would push the region further towards the right, hand US President Donald Trump a powerful ideological ally in its largest country and potentially strengthen Washington’s hand as it seeks to counter China’s influence across the hemisphere.
articles.body: Brazil is heading for another Lula-Bolsonaro showdown. But this time it is Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son Flávio who stands between leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and another term in power. A Bolsonaro victory would push the region further towards the right, hand US President Donald Trump a powerful ideological ally in its largest country and potentially strengthen Washington’s hand as it seeks to counter China’s influence across the hemisphere. For Lula, 80, the runoff vote leaves one of Latin America’s most prominent left-wing leaders fighting for what is likely will be last term if he wins. Bolsonaro seems to be thriving without his father Together, Lula and Bolsonaro accounted for more than 92% of the votes, underscoring the strong grip of the Lula and Bolsonaro camps on Brazilian politics. But neither secured the 50% needed to avoid a runoff, now set for October 25. The situation now resembles that of 2022, but Bolsanaro performed better than his father did in the first round four years ago. The crucial battleground was the Southeast, where nearly 40% of the electorate lives. There, Flávio won São Paulo and Minas Gerais. His victory in Minas Gerais carries particular symbolic weight: the state has voted for the winner in every presidential election since 1989 when Brazil held its first direct presidential election after military rule. The result suggests Bolsonaro, who exceeded poll projections, has done more than simply inherit his father’s political movement. He may have expanded it. With a campaign focused on crime and the economy, he secured nearly four percentage points more than his father in the first round in 2022. He leaned heavily on his father’s image while also seeking to present himself as a more moderate figure. For Lula, the result raises an uncomfortable question. Can his political legacy and record in office still deliver an electoral majority? Minas Gerais helps explain his predicament. He received 43.21% there, well below the 48.3% won in the first round of 2022. Nor did he achieve the lead margin his campaign had hoped for in the Northeast, his main stronghold. The race is far from over The runoff will depend on who can capture voters who backed eliminated candidates and whether either side can mobilize Brazilians who stayed home on Sunday. The eliminated candidates collectively accounted for 7.82% of votes. Most of those votes went to candidates on the center-right or right, potentially giving Bolsonaro another advantage. But abstention is another potentially decisive reservoir of votes. About 21% of eligible voters did not cast a ballot, and mobilizing them could tip the scales in a tight election. Polls leading up to Sunday showed the two candidates tied in runoff scenarios. Lula must now overcome a first-round deficit amid voter concerns over purchasing power and crime, an issue Bolsonaro made central to his campaign, as well as controversies surrounding key figures in scandals seen as close to the president. Bolsonaro, meanwhile, enters the runoff with another advantage: political momentum beyond the presidential race. His party and allies won numerous Senate seats as well as governorships in key states, potentially giving a Bolsonaro presidency significant legislative and regional support. An even more polarized runoff is expected. Lula will likely frame the vote as a referendum on democracy and while Bolsanaro will focus on his tough-on-crime rhetoric and allegations of corruption against Lula and his party. Trump has plenty at stake Few outside Brazil have more riding on the runoff than Trump. The US president openly endorsed Bolsonaro earlier in the campaign and maintains a tense relationship with Lula’s government. He has been notably quieter in recent weeks but there is little ambiguity over which outcome would better suit Washington. Since Trump returned to the White House, no left-wing candidate has won a presidential election in Latin America. Now, Washington hopes to bring about an ideological shift in Brazil, the region’s biggest economy, that will help it fully impose its “Donroe Doctrine” and contain China’s influence. “Trump had already welcomed Bolsonaro to the Oval Office at the White House and has imposed punitive tariffs on Brazil, the sole motivation for which appears to be political,” international relations expert Farid Kahhat, a professor at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, told CNN. “The fact that he hasn’t spoken out publicly again doesn’t change the fact that he already did so in the past and that he has made public policy decisions in favor of the Bolsonaros,” he added. For Kahhat, Trump’s recent restraint may itself be strategic. “They’ve already decided it was better to keep a lower profile,” he said. There is good reason for caution. Open intervention by Trump could have the opposite effect in the world’s tenth-largest economy, which is far less dependent on Washington than some of its neighbors. “They’ve noticed that in Brazil, [interference] might not work the same way as it does in Honduras or Colombia,” Kahhat said. Lula has also used the banner of national sovereignty as a campaign weapon. Political scientist Manuel Alcántara Sáez, director of the International Center for Political and Social Studies (CIEPS-AIP) in Panama, said another Trump intervention could end up helping Lula. “It would be more beneficial for Lula because there is a stronger sentiment against US interference,” he said. Trump isn’t the only regional ally to have backed Bolsonaro. Argentine President Javier Milei supported him and attended his campaign launch, where he hurled insults at Lula. “Since then, I haven’t noticed Milei getting so involved in the campaign,” Alexander Main, director of international policy at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, told CNN. “I think maybe they felt it wasn’t helping that much.” But Bolsonaro’s strong showing quickly drew celebration from the Latin American right. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella who won in June with Trump’s backing said on X: “May God have mercy on our brother country as He did on Colombia. True change is defeating the left.” Milei followed by congratulating Bolsonaro, saying: “The American continent is made up of citizens who want to live in freedom.” Is Latin America really moving right or just voting governments out? Bolsonaro’s performance appears, at first glance, to fit neatly into Latin America’s broader rightward turn. But analysts caution that something more complicated may be happening. With strategies based on antagonism and the “cancellation” of the opponent, policy proposals and promises “matter very little” in convincing undecided voters, Alcántara Sáez said. Beyond the committed bases, “the rest of the electorate is driven by other kinds of impulses, including fatigue and despair at seeing, on one side, an 80-year-old candidate and, on the other, a candidate who is the son of someone in prison, convicted of leading an attempted coup,” he said. That fatigue echoes a broader pattern across Latin America: incumbent parties struggling to survive voter frustration. Kahhat said that although “this is a time of crisis for the left throughout the region,” the string of right-wing victories should not necessarily be read as a wholesale ideological conversion. “It depends on the context, but it is not necessarily a rejection of left-wing movements as such, but rather of those in power at a time of great economic instability,” he said. Brazil’s runoff will therefore test two competing explanations for the political transformation sweeping the region: whether Latin America is undergoing a durable shift to the right, or whether frustrated voters are simply punishing whoever happens to be in power. For Alcántara Sáez, there is another dividing line that may prove just as important: how Latin American governments position themselves toward Trump. “Lula would clearly represent someone who would never in his life go along with the ‘Shield of the Americas’ initiative, whereas Bolsonaro would,” he said, referring to a political and security initiative floated by Trump. “So, rather than a shift to the right, I think this pro-US or anti-US. dimension is what we should be looking at more closely.” That makes October 25 about considerably more than who governs Brazil. The result could help determine whether the region’s largest power acts as a counterweight to Trump’s vision for the hemisphere, or becomes one of its most important allies.

articles.title: A box of old games donated to a Texas Goodwill contained a rare 1982 Air Raid cartridge for the Atari 2600; Goodwill said only 13 copies were known at the time, and the game sold for $10,590.79
articles.summary: A box of old video games donated to a Goodwill store in Texas turned out to contain a rare 1982 Atari game that collectors had been searching for.
articles.body: A box of old video games donated to a Goodwill store in Texas turned out to contain a rare 1982 Atari game that collectors had been searching for. The game, Air Raid for the Atari 2600, was sold at auction for $10,590.79 after a bidding war attracted 34 bids.According to Inside Edition,the rare find was discovered in early June 2021 at a Goodwill store in North Texas. Alex Juarez, an e-commerce item processor at Goodwill North Central Texas, was going through donated video games when he noticed one that looked different from the others.The game had a distinctive T-shaped handle and light-blue colour. Juarez recognised that it might not be an ordinary Atari game, so he called his father, who is a video game enthusiast. His father confirmed that the game was something special.The game was Air Raid, a title released in 1982 for the Atari 2600. It was manufactured by Men-A-Vision and was based on a simple premise in which players controlled an airship while defending Earth.Air Raid was not widely released. Its scarcity made it highly sought after by retro video game collectors. Goodwill North Central Texas said at the time that only 13 known copies of the game existed.The organisation did not know who had donated the game. According to Goodwill, the donor was most likely unaware that the old video game was a rare collectible worth thousands of dollars.Rare game goes up for auctionAfter Juarez identified the game, Goodwill North Central Texas decided to put it up for auction rather than sell it through one of its regular stores.The auction began on June 10, 2021, on the ShopGoodwill website. It was scheduled to run for seven days, but interest in the rare Atari game grew quickly after it was listed.The first bid of $20 came just 15 minutes after the listing went live. By the end of the first day, the bidding had already crossed $2,000.The offers continued to rise during the following days. By the morning of the final day, the highest bid had reached $5,100.The listing attracted considerable attention from collectors. Goodwill said the game was added to 235 watchlists during the auction.The biggest jump came in the final minute. The leading bid increased from $6,300 to the final sale price of $10,590.79. The result surprised Goodwill officials, who had expected the game to sell for considerably less.Liz Confiliano, director of community engagement at Goodwill North Central Texas, said the organisation had looked at previous sales to estimate the value of the game. The most recent copy they could find had sold on eBay in 2011 for $3,575.The Goodwill copy did not have its original box, so the organisation expected it to sell in roughly the same range. Instead, the final price was almost three times the amount of that earlier sale.$10,000 sale to support Goodwill programmesThe money raised from the auction was also set to support Goodwill's community programmes. Goodwill North Central Texas said the more than $10,000 generated by the sale could fund day habilitation services for one adult with disabilities for a year. It could also support job placement services and community resources for 20 homeless people.The organisation said the money could alternatively help 10 at-risk young people earn their GED while receiving a paycheck.Rosemary Cruz, vice president of donated goods and retail at Goodwill North Central Texas, said the organisation was having fun with the unexpected discovery. articles.title: Spanish PM Sánchez calls November election amid growing housing protests
articles.summary: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election after facing mounting pressure from mass protests over the country’s housing crisis.
articles.body: Spanish Prime ⁠Minister Pedro Sánchez on Monday called ⁠an ​early ​election in an apparent effort to seize the initiative following nationwide protests over a housing crisis sparked by the eviction of a 87-year-old woman. The election, scheduled for ​November ⁠29, will bring the current parliamentary term to an end more than six months ahead of schedule. “After informing the head of state, I have decided to convene an extraordinary meeting of the Council of Ministers this morning to dissolve Parliament and call a general election,” Sánchez, leader of the Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE), said in a televised address from Moncloa, his official residence in Madrid. The announcement came after Sánchez’s government last week failed to secure parliamentary backing for two propsoed laws aimed at tackling the country’s housing crisis. The measures were proposed following mounting public anger at the eviction of Maria del Carmen Abascal, known in Spain simply as Maricarmen, an 87-year-old resident of Madrid’s Retiro neighborhood, whose case has become a symbol of the country’s housing emergency. Maricarmen had been living in the same house for more than 70 years but was evicted after her rent increased from €500 ($560) to €2,650 ($2,970). Thousands of people took to the streets in fury, and she has become the face of the ruthlessness of Spain’s housing crisis. For more than a week, hundreds of people have camped out in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol to protest the crisis, and rallies have taken place elsewhere in Spain. Madrid’s Tenants Union, one of the groups organizing the protests, claimed about 950,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country over the weekend. Sánchez, who has been prime minister for more than eight years, called the election three days after right-wing parties in parliament defeated proposed laws aimed to ease the hosuing crisis. Analysts expect Sánchez to focus on housing in an effort to win over popular support. The conservative Popular Party, which opposed the ptoposed housing reforms, is leading in opinion polls. “We need to renew people’s support,” Sánchez said on Monday. “We need to mobilise and win a much larger progressive majority in parliament, one that will allow us to overcome vested interests, deliver new social advances and continue transforming Spain.” Sánchez’s socialist PSOE party has suffered several setbacks in regional elections this year, and a series of corruption scandals involving close associates have also tarnished its reputation. The migration crisis in Ceuta - in which tens of thousands of migrants crossed into the Spainish terriority bordering Morocco - during the summer intensified that criticism. “I know that among part of that social majority there is dissatisfaction today,” he said. “You are outraged to see their interests being trampled on in Parliament for the benefit of a select few.” As he called for snap elections, he conceded his government had made some “mistakes” but argued it had been faced with unprecedented challenges from abroad. He cited the war in Ukraine and the conflicts in the Middle East, he also highlighted Spain becoming one of Europe’s strongest economies. Sánchez is one of few left-wing leaders in Europe, as the right surges Sánchez is one of the few center-left leaders in Europe amid a surge in right-wing populism, and he has taken a firm stand on issues such as Palestinian statehood, the responsibility of social media companies and the US campaign against Iran. Spain refused to allow US bombers to use bases on its territory. Sánchez has been outspoken in his criticism of US strikes, provoking anger and threats from the White House. But rather than back down, Sánchez and his government doubled down, winning public support for his opposition to the Trump administration. In March, Trump threatened to cut off trade with Spain. “We could use their base if we want, we could just fly in and use it, nobody’s going to tell us not to use it,” he said. In contrast to much of Europe, Sánchez has also said that immigration is essential to sustain economic growth and moved to regularize the status of hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrants in Spain earlier this year. “I trust my fellow citizens,” Sánchez went on to say. “I know that you are a courageous and compassionate people who rise to challenges, and that you have no qualms about being the first, and the last, to stand on the right side of history.” Sánchez has put together a series of coalitions with left-wing parties and small separatist parties over the past eight years but has struggled to get legislation through at times, often falling back on decrees. The government has been unable to pass a budget for three years. Opinion polls suggest a coalition led by the center-right People’s Party (PP) with the support of the far-right Vox party is the most likely outcome in the election. If Vox were to join an incoming government, it would be the first time the far-right would be part of a government in Spain since the return of democracy after the death of dictator Francisco Franco in 1975.

articles.title: Pakistan installs fishing nets at security outposts to block drone attacks
articles.summary: Strung several metres overhead, the nets are a low-cost solution in sensitive areas prone to attacks by armed groups.
articles.body:
Hangu, Pakistan – Police officer Fayyaz Khan and his colleagues ducked for cover as drones carrying explosives rained them down on their checkpost in northwest Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province this year.

The April 16 attack was claimed by Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), commonly known as the Pakistan Taliban, and its fighters then opened fire from all sides of the Sarki Piyala police checkpost in Hangu district, about 30km (18 miles) from the border with Afghanistan and a hotbed of deadly attacks by armed groups, mainly the TTP.

The confrontation lasted roughly seven hours, killed the driver of an armoured vehicle and injured a constable, Khan, a 40-year-old police inspector, recalled.

“There was a great deal of fear because we were in the middle of a battle. At that moment, we did not even know whether we would make it back home alive,” Khan told Al Jazeera.

To defend against such attacks, the police in Hangu came up with an unlikely, low-cost solution – fishing nets strung several metres overhead between the checkpost’s rooftops and perimeter walls, forming a kind of aerial ceiling.

Simple in construction and resembling what fishermen use for their work, the netting was first installed two months ago, according to the local police. Since then, Khan said, no drone attacks have taken place at Sarki Piyala.

“If a drone comes over the checkpoint, there is a possibility that it could get caught in the net and be defused or stopped,” he said as his colleagues, strapped into bullet-resistant vests and holding guns in their hands, kept watch beneath a canopy of black mesh patched together with rope and wire.

“Even if a drone does not get caught and explodes above the net, the damage is expected to be much less because most of the shrapnel and fragments would be dispersed in the air rather than falling directly onto the ground where the police personnel are positioned.”

A standard checkpost can be covered with such nets for about 400,000 Pakistani rupees ($1,435), Hangu district police officer Tariq Habib told Al Jazeera.

“The police have introduced the netting system at vulnerable police stations and checkposts to reduce the impact of drone and quadcopter attacks,” Habib said, adding that more nets were being installed at police stations across the district.

He said the police in Hangu have asked for additional funding from the provincial government to expand the programme and their request is under review.

A spokesman for the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police said the nets have been installed at checkpoints and police posts in at least five other vulnerable districts: Kohat, Karak, Bannu, Lakki Marwat and Dera Ismail Khan. Even military outposts at some sites in the province have deployed the antidrone netting system.

The fishing nets have been put up in response to a shift in the tactics of armed groups, which are pairing gunfire and mortars with drones and quadcopters.

Pakistan has seen an increase in armed attacks in recent years, mainly targeting the police and the military, with many of them claimed by the TTP, which says it is fighting for a Taliban-style, religious-driven government in Pakistan.

Pakistani officials have repeatedly accused Kabul’s Taliban government of providing the TTP a safe haven on its soil and have demanded that it prevent cross-border attacks into Pakistan. Kabul has denied the accusations and called the attacks Islamabad’s domestic security problem.

In Hangu, the deadliest of such attacks happened on July 29 when attackers stormed a police outpost with quadcopters rigged with bombs before launching a ground ambush, killing at least 11 police officers and wounding 28. Fifteen attackers were also killed in the hours-long assault, claimed by the TTP.

On September 20, another exchange of fire in Hangu killed six soldiers and eight attackers, according to the Pakistani army.

That attack came two days after another armed group, called Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, killed 23 people, including 16 police officers, and bombed a mosque in coordinated attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Kohat district.

Police said they have recorded at least 16 attacks in Hangu this year, making it one of the most sensitive districts in the province.

But police officer Zeeshan Khan said no drone or quadcopter attacks have occurred at Sarki Piyala and the nearby Baliamena checkposts since the fishing nets went up.

He said the nets provide “an extra layer of security” to police personnel.

“If an attack does take place, the arrangements we have made can reduce the potential damage,” he said, estimating that the measures could reduce potential losses by 40 to 50 percent.

The frequent armed attacks have reshaped the daily lives of the people in Hangu who live near the police checkposts.

Mohammad Usama, a 28-year-old social activist in Baliamena, said the attacks often prompt families to pull children out of school.

“There is always a fear that a stray bullet or something else could hit our children, brothers, cousins,” Usama said.

“We just pray that Allah ends terrorism in our country so that we can live peacefully in our area, our children can continue their education and people can go to work without fear.”

Usama said since the fishing net was put up in his area, he has noticed a decline in ambushes.

But security experts said the strategy may offer a “false sense of security”.

“Deploying nets at particular locations is an immature, cheap ploy because police stations are not necessarily always the target,” Imtiaz Gul, executive director of the Islamabad-based Centre for Research and Security Studies, told Al Jazeera.

“The drones are intended to hit prominent locations and generate dramatic optics.”

He said the more pressing question was whether Pakistani security institutions have the capacity to intercept drones as soon as they take to the air.

“Drones are a source of scare and terror, and they can generate this intended spectacle whenever they are able to hit a strategic, important public location,” he said.

Fida Adeel, a Peshawar-based analyst specialising in counterterrorism and security, said the fishing nets are not a new concept. He traced them to camouflage nets used by the military to conceal their equipment. More recently, he said, they were adapted in Ukraine as a way to intercept Russian drones.

Adeel cautioned that the effectiveness of a fishing net against explosive-laden drones depends on its design and deployment. He also questioned whether the police estimates of “40 to 50 percent protection” could be verified without real-world trials.

“The extent of protection can only be determined through proper testing,” he said.

In response, Abdul Salam Khalid, a spokesman for the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police, told Al Jazeera they conducted a formal trial of the netting system in Kohat. He said an explosive was dropped on one of the nets during the trial, but it did not explode.

Back in Hangu, police inspector Khan said he knows that having fishing nets over his head is no foolproof solution. For him and his colleagues, he said, the nets offer some reassurance, even if they cannot eliminate the risks they face while on duty.

“We cannot say that the netting system provides complete protection,” Khan said.

“We remain prepared for an attack. … If defending our country and our people requires us to make the ultimate sacrifice, we will not hesitate. and we will not step back from our duty.”

articles.title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor takes legal action against UK police over Epstein arrest
articles.summary: King Charles’ younger brother Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has launched legal action against police in England over his arrest earlier this year on suspicion of misconduct in public office following revelations from the Epstein files in the United States.
articles.body: King Charles’ younger brother Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has launched legal action against police in England over his arrest earlier this year on suspicion of misconduct in public office following revelations from the Epstein files in the United States. Mountbatten-Windsor, 66, has asked for a judge to determine if Thames Valley Police’s actions against him earlier this year were lawful. The development was first reported by Britain’s The Telegraph newspaper on Sunday. He has lodged a judicial review in relation to the search warrants that were executed at his home at the Sandringham Estate and his former home at Royal Lodge in Windsor. A court hearing will be held on Thursday, British media reported Monday. Thames Valley Police confirmed to CNN on Monday that it was “engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court” and would not comment further with legal proceedings ongoing. CNN has also reached out to the UK Judicial Office for comment. The former Duke of York became the first senior royal in centuries to be arrested in February, the latest extraordinary development in a yearslong scandal over his ties to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, which obliterated his reputation and has thrown the royal family into crisis. He was detained by police on his 66th birthday at his new home on his brother’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk, eastern England, on February 19. He was taken to Aylsham police station where he was questioned for almost 12 hours before being released under investigation. No charges were filed; police have said its investigation is still ongoing. Mountbatten-Windsor’s arrest came after the force previously said it was assessing whether the former prince had shared confidential information with Epstein during his decade as a UK trade envoy. Mountbatten-Windsor has vehemently denied any and all wrongdoing in his dealings with Epstein, and has denied any personal gain from his role as a trade envoy, according to British media reports. He stepped down from official royal duties in 2019 following a calamitous interview with the BBC over his friendship with Epstein. But headlines related to the late financier continued to plague the disgraced royal. In 2025, King Charles stripped his younger brother of his title as prince, following public outcry after the release of a posthumous memoir by Virginia Giuffre, a prominent accuser of Epstein who alleged that Mountbatten-Windsor had sexually assaulted her as a teenager. Giuffre – who the prince claims never to have met – died by suicide in April 2025 at the age of 41. In addition to denying all allegations against him, Mountbatten-Windsor has also previously insisted he never witnessed or suspected any of the behavior of which Epstein is accused.

articles.title: Average five-year mortgage rate hits 6% for first time in three years
articles.summary: The cost of a new fixed-rate mortgage has been rising in recent weeks as lenders face higher costs.
articles.body:
The average interest rate on a new five-year fixed mortgage deal has hit 6% for the first time in three years, figures show.

The cost of home loans has been rising in recent weeks, as lenders face higher costs amid international concern over rising prices, interest rates, and government borrowing costs.

It means home buyers and anyone renewing a fixed deal have seen about 1,500 mortgage deals priced below 5% vanish since the start of September, according to the financial information service Moneyfacts.

It described the situation as "brutal" for borrowers, with the average rate on five-year deals now at 6%, and at 5.98% on two-year fixed mortgages.

For borrowers, the interest rate on a fixed mortgage does not change until it expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it. The vast majority of homeowners and buyers have this kind of mortgage.

Since the Iran war began, global economic uncertainty has been pushing up the cost of deals.

Moneyfacts said that the biggest High Street lenders had made repeated fixed rate increases during September. Barclays increased selected fixed rates on four occasions, while HSBC, Lloyds Bank, Nationwide, NatWest, Santander and TSB each made three rounds of increases.

It meant that the average rate on a new five-year deal was at its highest since September 2023. On two-year deals, the average rate is at its highest since December 2023.

"Average fixed mortgage rates rising back to three-year highs will be disastrous news for borrowers," said Rachel Springall, finance expert at Moneyfacts.

"Borrowers who were hoping mortgage rates would stabilise will be disappointed."

She said that those coming to the end of a fixed deal would be "wise to seek advice and compare deals carefully".

Some lenders could allow people to lock in a rate three months before their current deal ends, while others could allow six months, she said.

Springall said rate rises were "inevitable" because lenders' wholesale funding costs had climbed as a result of rising gilt yields .

Interest rates - known as the yield - on government bonds have been going up, meaning it costs the government more to borrow over the long term.

The knock-on impact of this on the mortgage market has meant that the number of fixed-rate deals priced below 5% has plunged by 99%, from 1,494 since the start of September 2026 to nine now.

In contrast, the number of sub-5% variable rate mortgages has remained broadly stable, Springall said, leading some borrowers to chose deals that track the Bank of England's base rate.

Millions of mortgage-holders are coming to the end of their current deals in the next two years.

Just over five million homeowners should expect their monthly mortgage repayments to increase by the end of 2028, according to Bank of England forecasts.

Some may have expected rates to have fallen this year, owing to improved economic conditions, but the Iran war has upended many of those expectations.

It has also led to wider pressure on the cost of essential bills.

On Friday, drivers saw the average cost of diesel rise above £2 a litre in the UK for the first time, according to the RAC motoring group.

Domestic energy prices also rose by 4% at the start of October, and forecasters have predicted a 16% increase when regulator Ofgem sets its next price cap for January.

The government is under pressure to support those most likely to struggle to pay at the Budget later this month.

articles.title: A $30 painting, found in ‘dark corner’ of estate sale, fetches $1.35M at auction
articles.summary: An enigmatic oil painting bought at an estate sale has broken an auction record after it was confirmed to be the work of a celebrated American surrealist named Gertrude Abercrombie.
articles.body: An enigmatic oil painting bought for just $30 at an estate sale fetched more than $1.35 million at auction after it was confirmed to be the work of celebrated surrealist Gertrude Abercrombie. The 8-by-11-inch still-life was discovered in a “dark corner” of a Michigan home in July, according to Freeman’s, the auction house that brought the painting to market this month. An expert has identified it as Abercrombie’s “Alderman Merriam’s Shells,” which had been unseen in public for almost 75 years. Completed in 1951, the painting depicts a collection of ten seashells — a common motif used by Abercrombie, who is often described as American art’s “Bohemian Queen.” Over the next two years, it was exhibited at six of the painter’s solo exhibitions, then priced between $50 and $150. But the artist never sold the work, instead gifting it to a doctor in Kalamazoo, Michigan in exchange for medical services. The mysterious painting was then passed down through the doctor’s estate following his death, before eventually appearing at July’s estate sale. The lucky buyer, who has remained anonymous, is described by the auctioneer as “a longtime hunter of record albums and mid-century furniture.” Detailing the find, Freeman’s said the painting had been discovered “tucked in a dark corner of a hallway leading to the garage — overlooked by every other buyer that day.” Upon seeing the signature (reading “Abercrombie, ‘51”), barely visible against the dark background, the buyer took a $30 gamble. According to Freeman’s, they then diverted a family vacation to visit Milwaukee Art Museum, where an Abercrombie exhibition was on show. There, in an exhibition catalog, a 1952 news clipping showed a photo of the painting next to the real-life shells it depicts. The bargain hunter then took the artwork to Freeman’s auction house, which was one of the exhibition sponsors. Abercrombie expert Susan Weininger, an art history professor at Roosevelt University, later authenticated the work as genuine — and still in its original frame. The painting was subsequently cleaned by art restorer Julian Baumgartner, who, in a video documenting his work, described it as being in “perfect condition,” aside from some grime and clouded varnish on its surface. “It was drab, missing its life, but now cleaned, retouched, and revarnished, it’s alive and radiant,” he said. The painting had been valued by Freeman’s at $150,000 to $250,000, though bids at last Thursday’s sale far surpassed estimates, setting a new auction record for Abercrombie’s work. In 2025, Sotheby’s sold another of Abercrombie’s paintings, “Message for Mercy” for a then-record of $1.02 million, more than triple its high estimate. A largely self-taught artist, Abercrombie, who died in 1977, was renowned for her otherworldly, dream-like compositions. She was also known for hosting legendary salons at her home, in Chicago’s Hyde Park, where jazz stars like Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker often performed. Snail shells and seashells (along with owls, cats, mysterious doorways and, in her own words, “simple things that are a little strange”) were recurring themes of her work. They often appeared cracked or marked with holes and set against Abercrombie’s signature sparse backdrops, whether barren moonlit landscapes or deep black voids. Some of her other uncanny compositions placed shells beside cryptic flags and dominoes or, in cases like 1967’s “Snail Woman,” birthing abstracted female figures. Objects in Abercrombie’s highly autobiographical works usually symbolized parts of her own experiences and identity, rather than abstract ideas. “I always paint myself,” she once said. Freeman’s auction listing meanwhile suggests that shells “served as a talisman of friendship, typically gifted to those closest to her.” In a press release prior to Thursday’s sale, the auction house’s senior vice president Zachary Wirsum described the painting’s rediscovery as “magnificent.” He recalled telling visitors at the Milwaukee exhibition that Abercrombie’s paintings do, occasionally, crop up at estate sales. “Little did I know that one of those ‘once in a while’s would occur less than a month later,” Wirsum is quoted as saying.

articles.title: Libyan teachers’ strike escalates as union demands major education reforms
articles.summary: School year is on hold with teachers on strike and other unions threatening to take action.
articles.body:
Teachers in Libya have escalated their protests over salaries into an open-ended strike at public schools.

Protests began on September 13, the day the school year was due to start. Sit-ins were held outside schools and government buildings in the capital, Tripoli.

Two weeks later, Libya’s teachers union stepped up the campaign with a nationwide strike. It has kept students out of classrooms across the country.

On Sunday, several Libyan unions representing other sectors threatened to join the strike unless the government entered talks to address a cost of living crisis .

Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah of the internationally recognised Government of National Unity (GNU) in Tripoli met with cabinet members to discuss a response to this crisis.

Libya has struggled with economic and political instability since a 2011 uprising ended the rule of late Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi.

The strikes are occurring on both sides of Libya’s political divide: its western region, governed by the GNU, and its eastern region, which is under the control of renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar’s self-described Libyan National Army.

In April, the rival legislative bodies of both sides agreed a unified budget for the first time.

Teachers said they are facing declining salaries, unpaid arrears, insufficient benefits and deteriorating school conditions.

They demanded an immediate halt to what they called the “erosion of workers’ incomes”, citing deteriorating economic and living conditions.

Principal Muftah Khalifa told Al Jazeera Arabic that teachers were protesting against the government’s failure to respond to their repeated demands for higher and unified wages, health insurance and protection on and off school premises.

Teachers told the Reuters news agency they face problems ranging from a lack of computer labs to desks being too dilapidated to use. Staff and parents often have to pay for equipment themselves.

A key demand is the adoption of a unified pay system that would balance a large disparity in pay between workers in different sectors. It is a call that other unions have now rallied behind.

Libya’s unions said on Sunday that the system should take into account changes in the cost of living and the fluctuating dinar-US dollar exchange rate. Retirees have also called for the implementation of previous agreements on pensioners.

The unions said no “arbitrary or punitive” measures should be taken against workers, retirees or union leaders over their activities. They also called on Libya’s attorney general to act quickly against any corruption concerning public spending.

According to an education budget brief prepared by Libya’s National Council for Economic and Social Development with UNICEF, 91 percent of the education budget goes to salaries and the rest to school costs, such as equipment.

The education sector had 560,000 employees in 2024, including about 270,000 teachers in basic and secondary education, a huge number for a country with a population of about 7.5 million people.

In 2018, the GNU passed Law No 4 to regulate the salaries, allowances and benefits of these workers.

It also provides for health and social care, insurance against illness and occupational hazards, and protection for teachers and their families.

In September 2021, the GNU ordered pay rises in line with this law, but it did not resolve the issue of salary arrears.

Thursday’s strike announcement came after union chiefs and teachers’ representatives from western Libya withdrew from a meeting called by the Ministry of Education.

Ashraf Abu Rawi, head of the Tripoli teachers union, told Al Jazeera that the unions felt authorities had not taken the teachers’ demands seriously.

The teachers union has warned the Ministry of Education against reopening schools, saying such a move would only lead to further escalation.

The government has said the teachers’ demands are legitimate but the rights of students should also be considered.

Osama Abboud, a parent of two pupils, said the teachers’ demands were legitimate and parents backed them. But he also urged teachers to think of their students’ future and continue working without abandoning their demands.

Dbeibah’s meeting on Sunday with Finance Minister Rashid Boughofa and other senior officials focused on a proposal of a unified pay system to cover all sectors and state institutions.

But raising teachers’ pay would require a government decision, parliamentary approval and banking procedures. All of this would take time, given the legislative schism that has plagued Libya for years, according to Al Jazeera’s Ahmed Khalifa, reporting from Tripoli.

articles.title: We gather news cautiously — unless it’s something bad about Israel
articles.summary: It is good, heartening even, that the Times handled last week’s foiled hijacking with care and caution. Yet somehow, it seems no claim about supposed Israeli perfidy is too stupid, outrageous, or ridiculous to make its way into the Times.
articles.body:
When it comes to crisis events, a cautious pose is always the smart play for a news organization. You never want to get ahead of the story — to prioritize being first ahead of being right.

The problem with modern news media, however, is that this caution is selective.

A group of Israeli air travelers on a flight from Dubai to Israel thwarted an alleged hijacker last week, rescuing themselves and others from a potential 9/11-style attack. The assailant, the flight’s co-pilot, repeatedly stabbed the captain in the chest. The plane then dropped nearly 14,000 feet. During the attack, the captain was able, if only briefly, to broadcast a hijacking signal and unlock the cabin door. Passengers then stormed the cockpit and overwhelmed the assailant.

Images of the incident were soon broadcast on television and social media, including photographs of bloodied passengers. Israeli officials quickly characterized the attack as terrorism. At 5:44 a.m. Eastern Time , Israel’s Channel 14 posted video from the plane in which a passenger said they had taken “control of the terrorists.”

Roughly 30 minutes later, the New York Times characterized the attack this way : “A plane flying from Dubai to Israel was diverted after an altercation between the pilot and co-pilot, Israeli officials said.” Other outlets did the same, putting out vaguely worded breaking news alerts that badly undersold the gravity of the situation. Reuters specifically called the attack a “ pilot brawl .”

This was several hours after an eyewitness had used the word “terrorist,” the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office announced it was “treating the incident as a terror attack in every respect,” and Defense Minister Israel Katz described the event as “a jihadist terrorist attack.”

The Times and Reuters were savaged online, accused of whitewashing what had happened thousands of feet in the air. The Times, for its part, put out an overly defensive response, saying from its official public relations account, “Our headlines and live coverage contain all the facts we’re able to confirm as we confirm them. Unlike activists and partisans, we don’t publish speculation or unverified information.”

We shouldn’t scold the Times, Reuters, or others for playing it safe — reporting only what they could reasonably and confidently verify. We want our media to exercise restraint and act responsibly as a matter of habit, and especially for these types of events, when the stakes are so high. But the care shown on this foiled hijacking story could not contrast more sharply with the Western press’s regular mishandling of allegations against Israel.

The New York Times has, in particular, racked up a rather ignoble record in this area.

The Times was among the first in October 2023 to misreport that Israel had bombed the Al-Ahli Arab Hospital , killing 500. Israel did no such thing. The rocket was misfired by the terrorist group Islamic Jihad, according to a U.S. assessment, and it did not even hit the hospital. Rather, it struck a nearby parking lot.

A New York Times editor’s note later conceded that the early coverage relied too heavily on the say-so of Hamas. This is a repeated problem with Middle East coverage. After all, if you can’t trust a medieval death cult, then whom can you trust?

The Times also claimed about two months into the war that Israel had killed more women and children than Russia had killed in Ukraine since February 2022. Shamefully, the Times sought to launder the claim through a supposedly independent third-party source — which, surprise, relied on Hamas figures. The report fell apart nearly immediately, partly because the Hamas-provided figures were unverified and partly because the cited death toll was actually lower than those from other conflicts.

Later, the Times claimed that Gaza deaths had surpassed “any Arab loss in wars in past 40 years.” This was also false, and the paper eventually issued a correction .

The Times also published a front-page photo of a Palestinian child with cerebral palsy and presented him as the victim of an Israeli-induced famine , captioning him as born healthy and recently diagnosed with severe malnutrition. The paper later acknowledged that it had failed to verify the child’s medical condition before publication.

Then, of course, there were the rape dogs. The claim that Israeli police canines are trained to rape Palestinian prisoners appeared in a May 2026 opinion article by Times columnist Nicholas Kristof. Tellingly, no one on the news side of the Times has ever been able to corroborate that story. Executive editor Joseph Kahn later said he probably would not have published the piece in the news pages. It is still profoundly unsettling that the paper’s opinion editors would run such an implausible claim without verification.

It is good, heartening even, that the Times handled last week’s foiled hijacking with care and caution, waiting for the full picture to emerge before reporting anything definitive. That is the bare minimum of responsible journalism.

But where is this same seriousness when the allegations are directed at Israel? It seems no claim is too stupid, outrageous, or ridiculous to make its way into the Times, so long as it is aimed at Israel.

When the Times says it does not “publish speculation or unverified information,” that doesn’t seem to apply to Hamas’s cooked numbers and absurd claims, or to its unverified allegations of hospital bombings.

And does this standard of caution apply to the Times opinion desk? If so, Kristof and his editors have some explaining to do.

Becket Adams is a journalist and media critic in Washington.

articles.title: Cornell tipster speaks out and Supreme Court begins a new term: Morning Rundown
articles.summary: A Cornell student who gave police leads expresses dismay with how the case was handled.
articles.body: A Cornell student who gave police leads expresses dismay with how the case was handled. The new Supreme Court term begins with a climate change case. And all passengers are presumed dead after a medical jet crashed off Nantucket. Here’s what to know today. Cornell student who gave police leads in alleged rape says she feels ‘betrayed’ over handling A Cornell student who gave campus police leads in the alleged rape of Jane Doe about 24 to 48 hours after the incident in 2024 said she feels “betrayed” over how authorities handled the case. The student, who spoke to NBC News yesterday on condition of anonymity, said she first heard about allegations that Doe was raped as a rumor on campus. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. The student said she decided to go to police after she saw screenshots of a Chi Phi group message on Snapchat and because “it felt like the right thing to do if we could help this girl.” She said she walked them through everything she knew, including that fraternity members were messaging about the events of the evening with Doe and about potential witnesses. She also gave police secondhand information about drug use at Chi Phi and said she was familiar with the frat house and believed she knew where ketamine was alleged to be kept. Read what others told us. New Supreme Court term begins with a climate change case The Supreme Court kicks off a new term today, with the justices hearing an attempt by oil companies to throw out lawsuits alleging they should pay damages related to climate change. The case concerns a lawsuit brought by the city and county of Boulder, Colorado against Exxon Mobil and Suncor Energy. The ultimate decision could have broad ramifications for similar lawsuits around the country. Boulder officials say they face increasing costs because of the impacts of climate change, including efforts to minimize risks from wildfires. They accuse Exxon and Suncor of misleading consumers about the effect of greenhouse gasses from their products, an allegation the companies deny. Other major cases already on the court’s docket involve a challenge to bans on AR-15 semiautomatic rifles and two about the Trump administration’s hard-line immigration policies. Here’s what to know about oral arguments. 6 presumed dead after medical jet crashes off Nantucket The operator of an air evacuation jet that dropped off the map in waters off New England said that it’s facing “the heartbreaking reality” that all on board have died. Canada-based Latitude Air Ambulance said that the flight, which appeared to have crashed off Nantucket, Massachusetts, was carrying a patient, a family escort for the patient and four crew members. They were four Canadians and two Bermudians. A source familiar with the matter told NBC News the Bermudians were the patient and the patient’s son. Air traffic controllers lost contact with the jet early Saturday as it flew from Bermuda to Boston. The search for the passengers was suspended yesterday, after 66 hours of combing the seas, the U.S. Coast Guard said. Read the full story here. Russian lab worker dies of suspected plague as 200 enter medical observation Almost 200 people are under medical observation in Russia’s Siberia region after the death of a 28-year-old lab worker who may have been exposed to pneumonic plague, according to local media reports. While Russian authorities have not confirmed her exact cause of death, the country’s consumer welfare service said Sunday that the researcher at an anti-plague institute in Irkutsk had died of “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” or origin. It said the “sanitary-epidemiological situation” in the Irkutsk region and the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov was “stable.” The pneumonic form of plague is especially contagious and “can trigger severe epidemics,” according to the World Health Organization. The WHO did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday about the suspected case in Russia. Dr. Ashish Jha, who served as the White House Covid-19 response coordinator from 2022 to 2023, said “much more” information and transparency was needed from Moscow. “If there were weapons programs, biological weapons programs in these labs, that would be much more concerning to me,” he told NBC News in an interview. “We need to understand that now.” Read the full story here. NFL Week 4: Redeemed QBs and the AFC’s best (so far) Week 4 of the NFL season featured dramatic comebacks, quarterbacks who redeemed themselves (while others continued to struggle) and three teams left with undefeated records. Here’s all the action you need to know from yesterday: After coming under scrutiny for poor performance, Patriots quarterback Drake Maye had his best game of the season. He threw for 269 yards and three touchdowns, handing the Bills their first loss. Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert had three turnovers in a 30-23 loss to the Seahawks, dropping Los Angeles to 0-4.Are the Jaguars sneakily the best team in the AFC? They improved to 3-1 with a 22-17 win over the Bengals. Meanwhile, the best team in the NFC East is anyone’s guess.The NFL said it’s reviewing an interaction between an official and Arizona Cardinals tight end Trey McBride. Read more highlights. Staff Pick: Walmart’s fashion gamble This story was born after one of our executive producers noted her stylish cashmere sweater wasn’t from a fancy designer store but...Walmart! The big box retailer has been making waves as it embraces the fashion world with a new clothing and accessories line, dubbed “Scenario.” The company describes the brand as “bohemian” and “romantic,” which immediately caught our attention. Can that messaging really translate to the Walmart customer? How does a company famous for its ultra-low prices on everyday essentials rebrand itself into a fashion destination? And could this be a play to capture market share from Target? We hit the streets of New York to find out what shoppers really thought about the pivot — and whether there was any shame associated with the Walmart fashion game. Interestingly, most folks were all for it, citing value and affordability. That’s not totally surprising given the state of the U.S. economy, with consumers squeezed by high prices and inflation. Needless to say, the retail landscape is rapidly changing, but experts told me it will be an uphill battle for Walmart to shed its reputation of “cheap” and embrace a new mantra of “chic.” — Allie Canal, business and economy reporter Read All About It Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries that allow researchers to switch on and off nerve cells in the living brain. articles.title: Growing outrage in Japan after US Marine arrested in woman’s killing
articles.summary: The 20-year-old soldier denies the charge as protests held on Okinawa and in Tokyo.
articles.body:
Japan’s prime minister says the killing of a woman , allegedly by a US Marine stationed in Okinawa, is a “heinous crime”, and she has called on the United States to “thoroughly enforce discipline” amid growing outrage in Japan.

Sanae Takaichi told lawmakers on Monday that the government has urged the US to provide “full cooperation with the investigation” and called for “strict discipline among US military personnel”.

About 54,000 US military personnel, including 18,000 Marines, are stationed in Japan. The majority of these forces are based in Okinawa, a Japanese island that came under US administrative control at the end of World War II and was returned to Japan in 1972.

Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drink-driving incidents by US personnel have long sparked protests on the island.

The new case involves a 20-year-old Marine who was arrested on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old woman at a hotel in the city of Naha and stealing her wallet, police said on Sunday.

The Kyodo News agency, quoting police, reported that the woman’s body was found in a hotel room and she appeared to have been strangled.

The Marine was arrested by Japanese police on Sunday and sent to prosecutors on Monday, according to Kyodo News. He has denied the charges.

“The occurrence of such a heinous crime is extremely regrettable,” Takaichi said.

Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told reporters on Monday that Tokyo will “continue to urge the US side to thoroughly enforce discipline” among its soldiers in Japan.

Kihara, who is in charge of mitigating the impact of US forces in Okinawa, said Tokyo has protested to the US at “various levels”.

The incident has caused outrage across Japan, and the Japanese Ministries of Foreign Affairs and Defence have summoned the US ambassador and the commander of US forces in Japan.

According to Jiji Press, about 100 people held protests outside the Okinawa prefectural government building on Sunday and shouted: “How much longer do we have to bear all of this?”

Another 100 people participated in a rally in Naha on Sunday, Japanese media reported.

Okinawa native Sorane Sakihama, 24, who organised a similar rally in Tokyo on Sunday, said she cried upon learning about the woman’s death.

“We couldn’t protect her. That made me so angry and sad,” the university student told the AFP news agency, adding that she was planning to organise another protest in front of the US embassy on Tuesday evening.

“I want to ask them: What are these soldiers stationed here for? They might say they are here to protect lives or boost security. But how can they say that when a life was taken by one of their own?”

Since Okinawa was returned to Japan, about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested in Japan, according to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper.
