articles.title: In 2019, a Thornbury couple won £1 million on EuroMillions while Natalie was eight months pregnant; days later, daughter Poppy arrived about a month early: ‘She wanted to join us for it all’
articles.summary: In February 2019, Natalie and her then fiancé Andrew Symes won £1 million in the EuroMillions UK Millionaire Maker draw.
articles.body: In February 2019, Natalie and her then fiancé Andrew Symes won £1 million in the EuroMillions UK Millionaire Maker draw. Just days after becoming millionaires, the couple also welcomed their second child. Seven years after winning the lottery, the couple spoke about the win, welcoming their daughter a month earlier than expected, and how their whole lives have evolved ever since. Their story comes as new data names Bristol as one of the luckiest places in the UK for lottery winners. There are now 100 National Lottery millionaires, while 669 players have won £50,000 or more on National Lottery games.An emergency shop visit and an impulse ticket purchaseIt was a Friday. Natalie was eight months pregnant and had a toddler. “I didn't know at the time, but I also had swine flu. So I was feeling pretty awful,” she told Bristol Live recently.As it was snowing badly, she grew anxious. “I could just see the snow getting worse and worse from our house in Thornbury. I was frantically ringing my fiancé at the time to say that he needed to get home in case the roads weren't clear and he wouldn't be able to get back. I wouldn't have been able to deal with our toddler myself in the snow.”Andrew Symes left work early and stopped at the local Tesco to grab some supplies in case the snow got worse. “I think he heard it on the radio in the car that there was a rollover jackpot on the lottery. He just decided to buy a ticket while he was in there,” Natalie recalled. The purchase was quite out of the blue. “We don't usually play the lottery. It was a real spur-of-the-moment thing,” she said. Andrew even joked with the man who sold him the ticket, saying, “I'll be back later, this is the winning ticket.” Turns out, his words were prophetic.The ticket was for the EuroMillions UK Millionaire Maker draw on Friday 1 February 2019. It was left on a shelf at home and almost forgotten. Natalie was jokingly waving around some cash from the sale of an old pushchair, pretending they were rich, when Andrew checked the ticket numbers and told her they actually were!The unexpected winMost people who buy tickets don't really expect to win. Natalie thought the same. “It's not something you ever expect to happen to you.” On the day of the result announcement, Andrew checked the ticket and was surprised.“We're huddled around his computer screen and we didn't believe what we were reading. Neither of us knew what to do next, because obviously it's never happened to us before and it's not something you ever expect to happen to you,” she recalled.She sent Andrew back to Tesco with the ticket. The same man who sold it was on the till. He scanned the ticket and told Andrew to ring Camelot, the operator at the time.“We rang. They confirmed it. And we were in disbelief. It didn't seem real. Before we spoke to the woman on the phone, I thought it was all a prank or something.”A new lifeThe couple were living in a bungalow and owned no property at the time. So a home of their own was the obvious first purchase. By the weekend, they were touring new builds. While they were shopping for homes, their daughter Poppy thought this was the best time for her to arrive on Earth, and that too a month before her due date.“We won on the Friday and we went to look at a few of the new builds nearby on the Sunday. And I remember not being able to go up the stairs, because I was having lots of pain. I thought maybe my daughter had just moved around and she was in an uncomfortable position. I didn't really think too much of it, but then that didn't go away, and I ended up going to the hospital on Monday. Labour must have started while we were house viewing and she was born at 36 weeks - a whole month early,” she revealed.Poppy arrived on 5 February, four days after the draw. “She did want to join us for it all!”They won the lottery at the right time. With lockdowns arriving the following year, Andrew, a payroll supervisor at a pensions firm, might otherwise have spent them working from a cupboard under the stairs. The money also covered the couple's wedding and a second property, which now brings in extra income. The lottery money changed their lives for the better. Natalie can now be at home with the children, something she thought she'd never manage.“They were all just pipe dreams at the time, but now we're married and have our own home, and I can do the school runs and see the school plays and, if I'd have been working, I wouldn't have been able to do all that. It also helped relieve some pressure during the Covid lockdowns, which was nice,” she said.Plenty of lottery winners keep it quiet. Natalie rang her mum straight away.You use AI every day. articles.title: WMA members must call for release of detained Palestinian medics
articles.summary: All World Medical Association members have a duty to uphold their commitment to the protection of healthcare workers.
articles.body:
More than 1,700 healthcare workers have been killed during the genocide in Gaza. Israel has detained hundreds more without charges. Doctors, nurses and paramedics who stayed to treat the wounded have themselves become casualties of this war.

When medical staff are killed, imprisoned or disappeared, it is not only they who pay the price. Patients lose the people they rely on to keep them alive.

This is something delegates who gather in Rotterdam this week for the General Assembly of the World Medical Association (WMA) must remember. The fate of their Palestinian colleagues should be put on the table, not as a debating point, but as a test of whether the world’s governing body of medical ethics still means what it says.

The WMA already recognised the seriousness of these issues last year by adopting a resolution on the protection of healthcare in conflict. That was an important step and a welcome reaffirmation of the principles of medical neutrality. The challenge now is to ensure this is followed by the commitment of every medical association to explicitly support it and to use its influence to pressure governments to act.

If the WMA Assembly needs a single face for this file, it could be the one of Dr Hussam Abu Safia, the paediatrician who was the head of Kamal Adwan Hospital, the last functioning hospital in northern Gaza until Israeli forces stormed it in December 2024.

He’s been held now for more than 22 months without charge under Israel’s Incarceration of Unlawful Combatants Law, which permits indefinite detentions. He reportedly continues to endure prolonged solitary confinement, beatings, severe weight loss and untreated pre-existing conditions. An international petition for his release has drawn the signatures of more than 970 medical professionals from 41 countries.

Alongside him stands Dr Mazen al-Rantisi, the 71-year-old family physician from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, known as the “doctor of the poor”. He was arrested in June in a predawn raid on his home.

In addition, our longtime Doctors Without Borders (MSF) colleague, Dr Mohammed Hassan Ali Obeid, a respected 43-year-old Palestinian orthopaedic surgeon and father of three children, has been detained under the Unlawful Combatants Law in Israel for more than 600 days without charge.

Although detained health workers have been released, more than 80 remain in Israeli custody alongside at least a dozen arrested from the West Bank.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has recorded 1,000 attacks on healthcare, which have resulted in more than 1,000 deaths and 1,700 injuries in Gaza since October 7, 2023. Roughly 90 percent of Gaza’s health infrastructure has been destroyed or damaged. In August 2025, United Nations experts stated that the systematic destruction of the health system amounts to “medicide”.

In the West Bank, where no wartime emergency provides cover, the WHO also documented more than 1,000 attacks on healthcare since October 7, 2023, with 42 deaths and at least 218 injuries.

Ambulances are stopped at checkpoints and their crews taken. Medics trying to reach people injured in settler attacks have themselves been obstructed. Dialysis and oncologic patients stay home because the checkpoints make the journey to treatment impossible. Healthcare workers have been shot, detained and killed during Israeli military raids.

All of this represents Israel’s deliberate and systematic endeavour to dismantle Palestinians’ capacity to provide care. This is consistent with its clear and blatant disregard for Palestinian life.

The WMA Assembly should speak plainly about what is happening. It should call publicly for the release of detained Palestinian doctors, including Abu Safia, al-Rantisi and Obeid. It should press for independent access to those still being held. And it should back independent investigations into attacks on healthcare in Gaza and the West Bank with the findings made public regardless of where they lead.

This is an opportunity to collectively pressure fellow medical associations, political authorities and any relevant bodies to take action.

What lies before the Rotterdam assembly is a duty. One that reaffirms loudly, structurally, universally the founding proposition of the WMA: that membership carries an ethical responsibility, which does not flex with geography or alliances.

Healthcare workers are not targets. Either a white coat is worth protecting everywhere, or it is protected nowhere. The test is not simply whether we affirm these principles, but whether we uphold them when it matters most.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: 30,000 ancient treasures saved from ISIS in daring archaeological rescue
articles.summary: A study by professor and author Maamoun Abdulkarim reveals how archaeologists rescued 30,000 priceless artifacts from a Syria museum before ISIS captured the city.
articles.body: A recent study is shedding light on how brave archaeologists risked their lives to save approximately 30,000 priceless artifacts as ISIS closed in on a Syrian city. Published in the journal Museum Management and Curatorship, the study details the rescue of the artifacts from the Deir ez-Zor Museum in Syria. The artifacts are described as "priceless and were saved from the museum before the city was captured by ISIS," news agency SWNS reported. Phys.org also reported on the study. ARCHAEOLOGISTS MAKE UNUSUAL FIND NEAR SITE WHERE ARK OF THE COVENANT WAS ONCE KEPT The Deir ez-Zor haul was part of some 300,000 museum objects rescued and relocated across Syria. The museum's collection spanned thousands of years of history. It included ancient statues, jewelry and cuneiform tablets, including numerous tablets unearthed at the ancient city of Mari. Although the rescues took place in 2014 and 2015, new details about the operation have only recently been revealed in the study by Maamoun Abdulkarim, said SWNS. HOLY LAND DISCOVERY REVEALS ANCIENT CHARRED RELICS FROM ONE OF JERUSALEM'S DARKEST CHAPTERS Despite not being one of the largest museums in Syria, the Deir ez-Zor Museum housed one of the country's most valuable collections. The museum held priceless treasures unearthed at some of Mesopotamia's most renowned archaeological sites, including Halaf, Dura-Europos and Mari. Abdulkarim, a professor of archaeology and history at the University of Sharjah in the United Arab Emirates, oversaw the operation as director-general of Syria's Directorate-General of Antiquities and Museums. He presented the rescue as a case study in protecting cultural heritage during wartime. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER In the study, he argued that carrying out such a rescue amid active hostilities requires far more than logistical planning. "It fundamentally involves decision-making, institutional resilience, trust and the ability to adapt rapidly to changing circumstances," Abdulkarim said, as SWNS noted. "There is rarely a perfect moment to act during an armed conflict; often, delaying a decision in search of greater certainty poses a greater danger than acting under uncertainty." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The rescue was fraught with danger, Abdulkarim said, as the museum was linked to a military airport by only a narrow and highly vulnerable corridor. The period when ISIS rapidly expanded its control in 2014 "formed a critical juncture, as it coincided with the fall of Mosul in Iraq, the looting of its civilizational museum and the destruction of antiquities from Nineveh and Assyria," Abdulkarim said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ He said those events prompted Syrian antiquities authorities to urgently reassess their protection plans and accelerate efforts to safeguard museums in cities at risk of siege or collapse. "In a cultural emergency, waiting for perfect conditions can become more dangerous than acting under uncertainty," Abdulkarim said. "It is also about when we decide to act, whom we trust and how quickly we are prepared to adapt."

articles.title: FlyDubai co-pilot allegedly planned to crash Israel-bound jet at Ben Gurion Airport
articles.summary: Hamam al-Hammami allegedly planned to crash FlyDubai Flight FZ1073 into Ben Gurion Airport, according to reports on the terrorism investigation.
articles.body: The FlyDubai co-pilot accused of attacking his captain in an attempted terrorist act aboard an Israel-bound passenger jet allegedly planned to crash the aircraft into Ben Gurion Airport, according to new reports on the investigation. Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 reported that Hamam al-Hammami told investigators he intended to continue FlyDubai Flight FZ1073 toward Israel as though nothing was wrong, obtain the necessary clearances to approach Ben Gurion Airport and then crash the aircraft into a building or another plane at the airport. The information reportedly came from investigations by Saudi and Emirati authorities into the incident. Israeli investigators have not questioned al-Hammami directly, according to reporting from Channel 12 and Ynet. FLYDUBAI CO-PILOT ACCUSED OF COCKPIT ATTACK WAS GROUNDED BY OMAN AIR BEFORE JOINING AIRLINE: REPORT Fox News Digital reached out to the UAE Public Prosecution and FlyDubai seeking confirmation of the reported findings. Reuters separately reported Monday that a source briefed on the UAE investigation said the Omani co-pilot had planned to crash the flight into Ben Gurion Airport. Two Israeli officials with knowledge of the investigation also told Reuters that al-Hammami said during questioning that he had planned the attack before he was hired by FlyDubai. The latest details follow last week's dramatic incident aboard Flight FZ1073, which was traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv when the co-pilot allegedly attacked the captain inside the cockpit. NETANYAHU PRAISES HEROIC BYSTANDER IN BLOODY COCKPIT ATTACK FOR PREVENTING ‘ANOTHER 9/11’ UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said investigators determined that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a terrorist act by attacking the captain with a crash axe and attempting to take control of the aircraft. Passengers and others aboard the flight ultimately intervened, and the aircraft was diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely. Al Shamsi has said the UAE investigation remains underway to determine the full circumstances and motives behind the attack, as well as any potential links to others. articles.title: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and riot police
articles.summary: The prefect of Pas-de-Calais says the 15-year-old's life is "not in danger" after the "very serious" incident.
articles.body:
A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators near a school in France, an official has said, as student protests continue across the country.

The "very serious incident" happened in the north-eastern city of Lens on Monday morning, according to the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, François-Xavier Lauch.

"The student's life is not in danger," he said, adding that the teenager was transferred "very quickly" to a hospital nearby.

Around 500 schools were partially or totally closed across the country on Monday amid student protests over the condition of school buildings and staffing which have led to clashes with police in recent days.

There are mixed reports in French media about how the boy came to sustain the injury.

AFP news agency, citing a police union source, reported that the student appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which exploded in his hand.

However, regional newspaper La Voix Du Nord quoted a girl who it said was near the teenager as saying he did not pick up the grenade.

"He didn't pick it up. I was there, I saw it. He didn't pick it up, he didn't catch it," she was quoted as saying.

When asked about the incident, Lens Mayor Sylvain Robert said the circumstances still needed to be clarified.

"Like you, and like many others, I have seen some videos showing the aftermath. But I did not see how the operation was organised, either by the police or by the students," he told French media.

A regional prosecutor said an investigation would be carried out by the French police watchdog, the General Inspection of the National Police (IGPN), "so all light can be shed on what happened".

The incident took place close to the Auguste Béhal high school, the prefect said.

Lauch said a "larger gathering" of students than on previous days had assembled outside the school.

"At the start of the morning, they threw various projectiles at the local police officers who were on site initially. When I say projectiles, I mean stones, fireworks, and mortars," he told French media.

"Instructions were given by the interdepartmental director of the National Police, naturally with my approval, to deploy a company of riot police (CRS) here to maintain order, and it was in this context that this event occurred."

The school issued a statement on Monday morning, saying: "In light of the events that took place this morning and in order to ensure the safety of the entire school community, the institution is switching to distance learning from now on.

"In addition, to support everyone during this period, a listening and support unit has also been set up at the establishment."

This is not the first time students have been seriously injured during the recent wave of protests in France. Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône after reportedly being struck in the head by a tear gas grenade.

The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has announced an investigation.

Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered".

"His jaw is wired shut. He can't eat except through a straw and only liquids," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying.

"It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," she said, adding: "This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study."

articles.title: Dawood Safi detained for killing Wayne Broadhurst in Uxbridge
articles.summary: Dawood Safi killed Wayne Broadhurst and injured two others in a knife attack in west London.
articles.body:
A man who killed a dog walker and attacked two other people in a "frenzy of violence" in west London has been given an indefinite hospital order for manslaughter.

Dawood Safi, 28, fatally stabbed Wayne Broadhurst, 49, in the street during a series of knife attacks which began at Safi's home in Uxbridge on 27 October last year.

Safi, who was having paranoid delusions and hearing voices, attacked his landlord Shahzad Farrukh minutes before killing Broadhurst, and also stabbed a 14-year-old boy.

At Southwark Crown Court, Mrs Justice Cutts said Safi, an Afghan refugee, had been "in a psychotic state" and recommended that he be deported, but said the final decision rested with the Home Secretary.

In her sentencing remarks, the judge acknowledged the "devastating" impact of the crime on Broadhurst's family, and added that he was "a hard-working and decent man who was deeply loved".

Cutts told Safi: "Wayne Broadhurst, a gentle and quiet man, had the misfortune to be walking his dog at the time.

"As he emerged from the alleyway on to the street, you set upon and killed him in a frenzied, random, and completely unprovoked assault involving stabbing him at least 14 times."

Broadhurst's partner, Ann Newman, told the court she had had a "future stolen from me" and described facing up to a daily battle with grief and loss.

Safi, who was born in the Kapisa province of northern Afghanistan, was smuggled in to the UK on the back of a lorry in November 2020 and lied about his age - saying he was 17 instead of 22 - to stand a better chance of asylum.

articles.title: Plaque to honour Bristol scientist who led Beagle 2 Mars mission
articles.summary: The plaque, unveiled at the M Shed in Bristol, recognises Colin Pillinger who led the 2003 probe mission to Mars.
articles.body:
A museum plaque has been unveiled in honour of the scientist who developed the Beagle 2 probe - the first British and European spacecraft to land on another planet.

The tribute, at the M Shed in Bristol, recognises the space probe landing on Mars on Christmas Day 2003 and honours the contribution to the mission of the late Bristol-born scientist Professor Colin Pillinger.

"He was exceptional," said UK Space Agency former chief scientist Chris Lee who worked on Beagle 2 with Pillinger. "He managed to get everybody excited about space exploration."

Another 12 plaques were announced earlier this year to be installed at a number of sites linked to the historic landing.

UK's first Mars landing honoured with 13 plaques

Mars mission boss remembered on launch anniversary

Lee was one of the Filton space crew who contributed to the Beagle 2 mission before he became a leading scientist for the UK Space Agency.

"We were at the time the principal place for space exploration in the UK and Colin came to us because of our experience," Lee said.

"He was always very positive, one of those can-do figures. Where we would see problems, he would see solutions."

The unveiling of the Beagle 2 plaque, located in the People Gallery at the M Shed, took place on Monday.

Bristol City Council's Head of Culture Philip Walker said they wanted to celebrate the achievements of Pillinger, who grew up in Kingswood, and his team.

"It's great to be able to celebrate his contribution to the city," he said.

Pillinger, who died in 2014, passed away before pictures of the landing site revealed Beagle 2 did not crash-land on Mars as had previously been thought.

But although the landing of Beagle 2 was successful, it was branded as a failed mission as it was unable to connect back to Earth once it landed.

The mission landing is still regarded, however, as an historic success for the European Space Agency which has subsequently influenced future exploration .

In the years that followed the Beagle 2 mission, the UK contributed significantly to flagship space projects, including the Rosetta comet chaser and the James Webb Space Telescope.

"Beagle 2 started the UK down the line of being able to do planetary missions and knowing it could engineer them," said Professor Mark Sims, who managed the Beagle 2 mission.

A more recent example is the ExoMars Rover, Rosalind Franklin, which is due for launch in 2028 with the aim of finding out if life has ever existed on Mars.

"It's a European Space Agency mission but the rover was built in Stevenage and it will land on Mars hopefully in 2030 and look for signs of life which is what Beagle 2 was aiming to do," Sims said.
